title: Fifteen voices
hookLine: Kabir, Farid, Namdev, Ravidas, Trilochan, Beni, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas, Jaidev and Bhikhan

lines: FIFTEEN NAMES, NO GURU AMONG THEM.

teach.b: Sikhs call them the bhagats, the devotees. Tradition says that when Guru Arjan gathered the hymns that became the Granth, he set the words of these saints beside the words of the Gurus.
Where their hymns appear, they come at the end of a raag's section, after the Gurus' own: under the same musical headings, read in the same voice by the same granthi, bowed to the same way.

teach.h: AT THE END OF A RAAG.
teach.b: In Raag Asa, at the start of Bhagat Dhanna's hymns, there's almost a roll call. Namdev, a calico printer worth half a copper coin, became worth a fortune. Kabir left his loom for love of the Lord's feet.
Ravidas, who carried dead cattle, let go of the world's pull. Sain, the barber, became a devotee. And Dhanna, a farmer, hears all this and gets up to give his own life to devotion.
That list doesn't open with a king or a priest.

teach.h: A ROLL CALL OF WORKING PEOPLE.
teach.b: It opens with working people, named by their trades.
The bhagat hymns sign themselves, too: near the end you'll hear Kahu Kabir, says Kabir, or Kahi Ravidas, says Ravidas.

The voices stay distinct. Their accents and languages differ; some lines sound like a village and some like a court. Yet in the Sikh telling there isn't a front section for the Gurus and a back shelf for guests.
The whole book together is the Guru.

how: In gurdwaras the hymns of the bhagats are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib with the same honor as the Gurus' hymns, and the bhagat hymns carry their singers' names.

o: fifteen Gurus who led the Sikhs in turn
fifteen hymns that open each morning prayer
the bhagats, saints whose hymns sit in the Granth

s: every hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib was written by a Sikh Guru
the bhagats' hymns sit inside it too, saints who were not Sikh Gurus.
where the bhagats' hymns appear, they come at the end of a raag's section
after the Gurus' own, under the same musical headings.
a hymn in Raag Asa names bhagats by their trades
a printer, a weaver, a man who carried dead cattle, a barber, a farmer.

games.q: you're gathering a holy book for a community. you have hymns from saints who were never part of it: a weaver, a cobbler, a farmer, a Sufi. what do you do with them?
o: leave them out; the book is for our own teachers.
print them in a separate appendix.
set them in the book, same music, same honor.
games.why: tradition says Guru Arjan set them inside, under the same raags, and Sikhs bow to the whole book as the Guru.

practice: Pick any three of the fifteen, Kabir, Farid, Ravidas, or any that catch your ear, and say the first quietly, letting it ring out like a bell; wait, then the second, then the third.
Don't try to know anything about them yet; just let each name be a person who once sang. If you pray, you can follow the three names with Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Fifteen voices. The bhagats, saints from many castes and backgrounds, whose hymns sit inside the Guru Granth Sahib beside the Gurus' own.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: a devotee. the singers of these hymns are called the bhagats.

carryVoice: Your line: fifteen voices, one guru. Many accents, one book. That's day seven hundred forty-seven.
